utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue where I left off, I should like to say the following: It is quite clear that the only means that I have at my disposal is a telephone and even that telephone, yesterday afternoon, wasn't working. But that's just a small detail. I don't think we can talk about any kind of equality of arms between the parties or any kind of trial, even before an illegal Tribunal of this kind, when there is absolutely no equality of arms, when one party only has the right to a telephone, whereas the other side has all the strength and power and everything here to construct these false accusations and indictments, and that is why I once again ask you to set me free, because I have the right to equality, to an equality of arms and to a defence. You know that the international pact on human and political rights and the European Conventions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm -- Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt you for this reason: There is a witness here, and we're in the middle of his examination. If we're in the middle of an examination of the witness, it's right to finish that and then, at an appropriate time, to deal with administrative matters. Now, the Prosecution, in this case, as I understand it, have some matters which they wish to raise. Mr. Nice, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I discussed it with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, there are some matters we wish to raise. I've discussed it with your legal officer just shortly this morning before you came in. It would be more convenient to be dealt with perhaps tomorrow than today, not least because a motion dealing with 92 bis is in the final stages of preparation and will be served, I hope, by lunchtime today. But it's obviously a matter that the Chamber, the amici, and the accused may wish to consider, and for other reasons tomorrow will be more convenient than today, although today is possible if that's what the Chamber would prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be convenient to deal with it after the next witness? Rather than fixing a time to finish another witness and then deal with those matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we will deal with administrative matters - and this will be the rule throughout the trial - at appropriate times. So what we'll do is we'll hear your applications after the next witness. If there are urgent matters, of course, you can raise them as you have done in the past, but on the whole, we should try and deal with the witnesses' evidence once they've started and finish it before we break it off. So if you will finish your cross-examination now, and we'll deal with the other matters tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is your cousin, your uncle's relative Naim Berisha? Is that his name?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am Agron Berisha, and I said at the start of my testimony that Naim Berisha is a close cousin, if we are talking about Naim Berisha, the doctor, who at the moment is living and working in Germany and who has been there for the last seven or eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Naim Berisha who was the head of the terrorist group of the KLA, who is your cousin on your uncle's side.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that the accused is confusing the Naims who have lived in Suhareke. The Naim Berisha who I mentioned is my uncle's son and lives in Germany and is a doctor by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you related to the Naim Berisha who it is said is connected to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean he's connected with the KLA now or was connected with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know a Naim Berisha connected with the KLA at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My cousin, the doctor, Naim Berisha, who is away, I said the truth. He is a doctor and works in Germany. I also knew another Naim Berisha who died in the war. He was a distant cousin of mine, and I didn't have any connection with him. I didn't know him personally. I only knew him as a face, and I know very little about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. That's the answer. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] All right. We've heard answers like this. One of the previous witnesses said that he didn't even know his own son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your cousin, this man Naim Berisha, do you happen to know that the killed policeman, Vranovci, whom I mentioned yesterday, and he was also an Albanian, was an uncle of his on his mother's side?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these things that the accused is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this man Naim Berisha, whom you say is a distant cousin, killed that uncle of his by the name of Vranovci?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Naim Berisha was a distant cousin of mine. There are about 150 Berisha families in Suhareke. I do not have close ties of blood with the person you have mentioned and I don't know anything about him killing an uncle of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is usually the state of affairs amongst you, that you have no connections. You talked about a cousin who was killed at a petrol station too. Did you know that that particular petrol station in your town was full of weapons and ammunition belonging to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cousin about whom I spoke was Jashar Berisha, and he too was a distant cousin of mine. Jashar, the late Jashar, was not killed; he disappeared. He was taken on the 26th of March 1999 by people whom I don't know. He was taken several hours after the events in the pizzeria belonging to the Shala family, in which the Serbian police killed women, men, children, in the cruelest fashion, and unborn children too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about the petrol station. It's suggested that it was full of weapons and ammunition belonging to the KLA. That is the suggestion which is made. Do you know anything about that? If you don't, Mr. Berisha, simply say "No."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you know how the people were killed in the cafe, when you weren't there either?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I explained very well. I didn't see these murders. These murders were related to me by people who were witness, who were eyewitnesses of this horror on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you are testifying to things that you have just heard about from others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he said that in his evidence. He said: I didn't see this, but I was told about it by survivors. Now, we understand that. We understand that, and this doesn't call for comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you claim yesterday that you watched somebody in front of a bus station killing a man or, rather, a man and a woman, a male and female person?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not right that I said that. I said that several minutes after I saw Nexhmedin Berisha wounded, seriously wounded and lying on the ground, and his wife, pregnant wife Lirie dragging him across the ground and putting him behind a shop in behind the shopping centre known as Malesia Reisen, a few minutes later, I saw a policeman looking at the ground and following some traces on the ground, and I'm supposing that he was following the bloodstains of the wounded Nexhmedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The policeman you saw, you saw him in front of the bus station. That's what you said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the bus station, and the police came out of a small door in the fence behind the bus station, following, it appears, the bloodstains of the wounded Nexhmedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw that, did you?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the policeman. I saw him watching the ground and walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I received information yesterday, while the phone was still working, that between your house and the bus station there is a building, Kosovovino, belonging to the Kosovovino company, and that from where you were, you couldn't see the bus station at all because of this building in between. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. The high building from which we're talking is about 200 or 300 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim, therefore, that from your house you saw the policeman at the bus station looking for that cousin of yours who was wounded; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the policeman was looking at the ground. And I supposed that he had found these traces of blood from the wounded Nexhmedin and was walking them -- walking along them. I am not sure what he was looking for or who he was looking for, and I only saw -- said what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you saw -- the only thing that you saw was the policeman walking and looking at the ground at the bus station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the bus station. I said that he came out of the little door in the fence round the bus station, and in the place where I had seen the wounded Nexhmedin, he started to look at the ground and to walk, looking at the ground. And he went in the direction in which the wounded Nexhmedin was dragged by his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far from your house and from where you were watching is it to the bus station?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventy to 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it is on the basis of you seeing the policeman that you concluded that he was looking for your cousin; is that it?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I supposed that he was following the traces of the blood of the wounded Nexhmedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are testifying on the basis of your assumptions. Do you happen to know -- do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours, a moment. I am not -- I am not here to make suppositions or to give my own views. I have come here to testify to what I saw with my own eyes. I saw how my cousins were killed in the most cruel fashion by the police, and I saw this event by -- with my own eyes, and I'm not going to deal with assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we understand that. As you'll appreciate, the accused is entitled to ask you questions about your evidence. If they're not proper or they're in the form of comment, we will not require you to answer. It may assist matters -- it's a matter for you but it may assist matters if you answer the questions shortly - "Yes" and "No" are sometimes sufficient - and we might be able to get on more quickly in that way. Mr. Milosevic, this is a chance for asking questions, as you'll appreciate, not for commenting on the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that I am asking the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but not making comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many policemen were killed before the aggression in the environs of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before which aggression?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before the NATO aggression, before the 24th of March, in fact.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call the NATO aggression an attack by NATO on the former Yugoslavia. It was not aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about that. Can you just answer the question whether you know how many policemen were killed before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about an event when, on the 29th of April, 1998, a person was killed? His name was Sasa Jovic, and he was a policeman, and he was killed at Dulje, which is very close to you.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Dulje is not far from Suhareke. It's about nine kilometres away. I don't know about this event, because at this time, on 29th of April, 1998, I was studying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the 17th of June, 1998, what about that, when, at the same spot, a policeman was killed, another one? His name was Sladjan Niric. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about it?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about another event that took place on the 24th of June, 1998, in the village of Birac? That's three kilometres away from Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't asked you what the incident was yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know about any incident that day. Yes, let's move on. When was it you said you got back, Mr. Berisha, to Suva Reka, from your studies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I returned the day after graduating to Suhareke. I graduated on the 25th, so I returned home on the 26th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you heard nothing about the incident in which seven people were killed, including a child, only three kilometres away from Suva Reka, one day prior to your arrival in Suva Reka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the event you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about another incident when, at Dulje, Dragan Tomasevic, Milos Stevanovic, and Goran Boskovic were killed, on the 8th of January, 1999? At that time, you were practicing as a doctor in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working at that time in Suhareke, but I hadn't heard about the incident you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about an incident in Sematista, nearby Suva Reka, when, again, on the 28th of March this time, 1999, Ivica Spasic was killed? He was also a policeman.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, I was with my aunt in Prizren. This was the time when I was forced to flee my home, and I stayed with my aunt for four days. So it was impossible for me to find out about what was happening in Suhareke, and still more in the village of Sematista.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume you know nothing again about the killing of seven policemen in Suva Reka at the beginning of April, or rather, in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we dealt with that yesterday. He was in Albania in April, and said, when he was asked about events then, that he knew nothing about them. Is that right, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you saw nothing of the bombing; is that right, or heard it either?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that after the beginning of the NATO attack, I didn't stay long in Kosova. In all, I spent three days in my home and four days with my aunt in Prizren. During this time, I didn't see anything of these bombings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. That's precisely why I'm asking you, because on the 24th of March, that is to say, on the first day, the repeater station Bukova Lala was bombed, near Suva Reka, and the whole of Suva Reka vibrated from that bombing. Is it possible that you could have heard nothing of that?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place about which you're talking, Bukova Lala, is a long way from Suhareke, deep in the hills, and above the village of Budakov. I didn't hear any detonation or thunder or great noise on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know it was during the night?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the bombings, the NATO bombings, started at 8.00 on the evening of 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about a residential block near the market in Suva Reka, which is 500 metres from your own house, and was hit by a bomb?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house is near the police station, near the bus station, and the place about which you're talking is in an entirely different part of the town of the Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Suva Reka is a small town. I suppose that when a bomb hits a small area of a small town, the whole town knows about this, and you're claiming that you know nothing of it. Well, just go ahead and say you don't know anything about it and we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need not answer this comment. This is not questions that you're putting to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When is it alleged that the bomb hit the residential block near the market? What date is that, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning of the bombing. I don't have the exact date. My phone didn't work yesterday afternoon, so I couldn't find this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Can we move on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the KLA attacks prior to the beginning of the aggression in the villages around Suva Reka, Rektina [phoen], three kilometres; Musatiste, six kilometres; Budakovo, five kilometres, Vranic, seven kilometres? So all of these villages around Suva Reka where the KLA attacks took place, do you know anything about these attacks?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know everything about the houses being searched when they were looking for weapons after these attacks. As far as I understood, you only know about the searches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter for comment, Mr. Milosevic, which you can make to us in due course. Yes. No need to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will now refer only to the time when you were in Suva Reka, which means starting with the 23rd of August, 1998, until the beginning of the aggression on the 24th of March. Do you know that 15 Albanian civilians were killed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of such an event you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This all took place in the area of Suva Reka where you resided.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time, I went from my home to my job and back home. All the time I was in Suhareke, I never went to the outskirts of the town. I said right at the outset I didn't see any soldiers of a KLA or any activity conducted by KLA. What occurred in the villages, I don't know, because I haven't been to those villages myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the end of May in 1998 until the end of June of 1998, Albanian doctors who worked in Belgrade all left Belgrade en masse?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear anything of it, did you?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was told that there was even a letter by the director of your clinic, stating that Albanian doctors at that time had left all together the clinic and went back to Kosovo. This took place in May and June of 1998.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently you have been misinformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that together with you doing the residential training, there were several Albanians. Did you remain? Did you remain at the clinic after they left?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there during all the month of June until the date was up for me to pass the test of graduation, which I took on the 25th of June. One week after me, Flora Belegu was also graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of them? Did they remain after you at the clinic?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June, the lessons ended. The academic year ended. So most of them left to go home on vacation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember when in March, prior to the NATO aggression, the KLA announced mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know about the monastery in Musatiste, a Serbian monastery from the thirteenth century?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there is a Serb monastery in Musatiste village. I don't think that it dates to the thirteenth century. I have never seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't worry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was burnt down?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know how many people were killed in the Suva Reka environs? Perhaps you learned of this later, upon your return. So how many people were killed prior to June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from Albania, which was on 28th of June, 1999, I found Suhareke destroyed and ruined. In the town of Suhareke, I saw about 50 per cent of the houses burnt down. Of the 50 villages of Suhareke, 49 were burned. Each and every house of them was burned down. I heard that during this war, Suhareke was deprived of 500 of its dear inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the facts concerning how many people were killed by the KLA in that area, since you know that a lot of people had been killed there? Do you know the figures? Do you know that, according to the records, 72 people had been killed by the KLA? This is what was recorded, and there are a lot of stories going about this as well. Out of these 72 people, 19 were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you anything about these KLA crimes, because it is obvious that you know nothing of this, especially as far as the bombings are concerned. Forty per cent of the bombings took place in Kosovo, and Kosovo represents ten per cent of the entire territory of Yugoslavia, which means that the majority of bombings took place in Kosovo, and you know nothing about this. This is obviously clear from what you stated. Did you go to Prizren after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he dealt with that yesterday, that -- Help us, Mr. Berisha. Did you see any bombing in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean NATO bombing, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that before the war, the residents in Suva Reka were mistreated and they seldom went out into the streets, and then after that, you said that the policemen confiscated the car of your friend, Fatani, but you also said that it was taken from him for several days. How many days later did they return the car to him?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not my friend; he was a cousin of mine, a close cousin of mine. He was killed on the 26th by the Serbian police and didn't have the good fortune to have his car back. The car remained at the police station in Suhareke. When I went to Albania, I saw the car there. I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said you went into town every day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to work every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody mistreat you, since you went into town every day?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to work every day, very afraid, in fact, but I was not mistreated. I already spoke about my mistreatment which happened on the 26th of -- 27th of June, when I was returning from Belgrade. 26th, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This cousin of yours, Fatani, did he belong to the family who had a gas station, the Fatani family who had a gas station in the village of Pirana?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Faton, and he didn't have any gas station. He was not the owner of any gas stations. He was an unemployed person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you because this gas station was hit by the NATO bomb, which caused fire in the village. You said that from the police station, they shot towards your house. However, you said that nobody was hurt and that in fact the policeman was simply demonstrating how far he could shoot. Did you see him doing that, showing how far he could shoot, or was there perhaps some other reason behind the shooting?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they fired at my home, someone fired at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Either toward your house or toward the area near your house, you said that a bullet went nearby. I think you said through the wall or through the window.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in the summer of 1998, someone fired at Ahmet Berisha in his home. The bullet entered his window and hit the back part of his room, the back wall of his room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that it was the policemen who did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on the next day and saw with my own eyes the hole from where the bullet entered and from where it left. I saw the trajectory of the bullet, which showed that it came from the police station in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is the Suva Reka police station?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From this area that was hit by this bullet that you just described.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that from every -- this bullet could have been shot from any point within the 100-metre diameter around it. Is it so or not, since you obviously very professionally concluded that this was the fact, this was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is not a question. It is a comment by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a policeman shoot at the house of your relative?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've -- Mr. Milosevic, I think we've exhausted this topic. Can we move on, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think this case is obvious. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put this question in general terms. Was anybody shot at in those days prior to the aggression? Was anybody shot at? Was anybody hit by a bullet in Suva Reka, a bullet shot by the police?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember well an event which occurred in Suhareke. It was the summer of 1998. That day, about ten persons were killed in the centre of Suhareke. First a worker, a Serbian worker, was killed, who worked in a state-owned shop in the centre of Suhareke. Nobody knew who killed him. I don't know his name, but I know that he was from Sopi village. Afterwards, the police killed eight, up to nine civilians in the streets and houses of that part of the neighbourhood in Suhareke. I remember this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw it? You saw this event?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see it myself because, at that time, I was working. The work where I worked was on the second floor of the hospital of Suhareke. I was with my patients and my nurses who were all very scared when we saw the dead Serb person brought to the clinic, and there was a lot of upheaval on the ground floor. I remember that we heard some fire shots on the ground floor of the clinic. We were really very scared. We closed the door of our ward and waited there for everything to boil down, to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who fired on the ground floor of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you inquire afterwards?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the situation calmed down, didn't you inquire about who was shooting on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps an attack of the KLA? I'm talking about this event when this Serb got killed and when they fired at the policeman, this event from the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said he was killed by unknown persons. We never learned who killed him. They were never discovered. He was a civilian. And I feel pains when I see civilians killed irrespective of what ethnicity they belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from my -- from what I gathered, you did not regret the killing of the director of your health centre, Mr. Vuksanovic. Yesterday, you said you didn't feel bad about his death because he was not a good person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've already gone over that. We're not going back to it. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you got anything else for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will expect you to bring the cross-examination to a close fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I expect that you will take an unbiased stance because I have a right to conduct my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have a right to conduct your cross-examination, but we also have a duty to ensure that this trial is concluded expeditiously, and that we will do. Now, you have a right to put your case to the witness. You have a duty to do so. But we note that there's a fair amount of repetition in what you've put and a fair amount of comment. So could you kindly ensure that these -- these matters are dealt with as quickly as possible. Now, let's get on with this and finish this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When asked whether you heard about some propaganda aimed against Kosovo Albanians, yesterday, as far as I can remember, you replied by saying that you had heard Vojislav Seselj saying -- saying the following, "We will expel all Albanians across the Prokletije mountains." Do you know where Seselj stated this?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I said yesterday I heard -- I don't remember whether I heard it on television or read it on newspaper or heard it from someone. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that he was speaking about the Albanians, or was he speaking about the KLA terrorists, if he said that at all?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that any functionary, representative of the government, or any official person of Serbia or Yugoslavia said something against the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember anybody having said such a thing, but it was a reality. It happened. We million Albanians went out of Kosova, and is it very important whether somebody said this or whether somebody didn't? Everybody knows that a million Albanians went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, if you'd confine your answers to just dealing with the question. There's no need to comment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the president of Macedonia, Gligorov, spoke about the route the Albanians should be expelled by. I did not understand the point of that explanation, so I'm asking you the following now: Are you saying that the leadership of Serbia, or rather, of Yugoslavia, made an agreement about this with Gligorov, the president of Macedonia? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. And also the statement of Gligorov, I don't know whether I heard it on television or I heard it from somebody or I read it in a newspaper, mentioning a corridor by which -- the Albanians should go through a corridor through Macedonia to be directed towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of an order by the KLA that everybody should leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that the only columns of Albanian refugees who were bombed by NATO were those who were returning and not those who were leaving Kosovo? None of the columns leaving Kosovo were bombed. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't talk about what I have heard. I will talk about what I saw with my own eyes. On that day, when I left for Albania, everybody was going in that direction. Nobody was coming back in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a slogan by the KLA: "Let's get out as fast as possible so that we can get back as fast as possible"?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember all the pamphlets in Albanian, appealing to the Albanians to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never saw a pamphlet of that kind, ever?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are ridiculous things that you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that Mr. May will caution the witness not to make comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that after establishing the Kosovo Verification Mission, the state of affairs changed radically.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the mission lasted six months?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about six months. I don't know exactly how long, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not important to know exactly, but do you consider that the situation had returned to normal in Suva Reka, completely?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the following conclusion is right and correct, dating back to those times -- or rather, the following observation, do you consider it to be correct? The observation is as follows: In the whole region - Prizren, Pec - that means that whole region along the Albanian border -- but let me read the full observation. In the whole region of Prizren and Pec, there were abductions being carried out and killings of Albanians loyal to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on orders from the command structure of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Milosevic, you've put this case thoroughly. We've heard what the witness has said. He said he knows nothing about this, and nothing is to be gained by repeating questions over and over and over again in a different form. Now, is there anything else on a new topic that you wish to ask this witness? Otherwise, we're going to conclude the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you are not allowing me to finish even my question. I asked the witness whether the situation changed radically for the better after the arrival of the Verification Mission, and he said yes. And I now quoted a portion of a report by the Verification Mission of the OSCE relating to the 5th to the 12th of March, 1999, in which it is officially noted that during that period, when he says he considers the situation was normal, that in the whole region of Prizren and Pec, there were abductions and killings going on of Albanians loyal to the SFRY, on orders from the command structures of the KLA, and I am quoting a report by that particular mission for the period that the witness considers the situation was normal and which refers to the activities of the KLA themselves, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. That question will be put. You've heard what Mr. Milosevic has read out to you. It is in relation to the period which you described earlier. Now, then, do you agree with the observations made in that report or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can reply about the situation in Suhareke because I said I didn't go out among the villages or in the towns mentioned by the accused. I can only talk about the situation in Suhareke, and at that time, people came out more freely into the town, some cafes opened, so that, more or less, the situation became more relaxed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can tender that report in due course as part of the evidence and we'll consider it, but there seems little point in going on with this witness with this line of questioning when you've heard the answers. Now, unless you've got anything else, we'll conclude it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have something else, yes, but at your insistence, I will skip this portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The period of the mission and the KLA activities, and when you say the situation was normal, you skipped over that, but you did note that the situation deteriorated rapidly when the Verification Mission was withdrawn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. After the international observers left, the situation became very serious, and it went back to the same it was that prevailed in my town in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that this sudden withdrawal of the Verification Mission was, therefore, a factor which had a negative effect on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the situation was normal during the presence of the Verification Mission and that after that, after it withdrew suddenly, the situation deteriorated. That's what you said. Now, do you consider that this withdrawal of the Verification Mission was a factor which had negative repercussions on the situation in Suva Reka where you, for instance, lived? I don't want to say Kosovo and Metohija, but in Suva Reka, where you in fact lived.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the very fact that the situation went in that direction shows that the departure of the international observers led to a deterioration of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I'm going to skip over all the questions that I wanted to ask with respect to concrete events, but I can't skip over all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you know that the provisional executive council of Kosovo and Metohija, at the beginning of the aggression, issued an order that every health centre should set up two medical teams for assistance to the refugees and the injured and wounded from the bombing. What did your medical centre do? Did it set up these two teams?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any medical teams such as you mention. I was a gynaecologist, and I was -- dealt with my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a gynaecologist, make up part of any medical team for assistance to the refugees and the casualties of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the NATO bombing, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean during the war, the whole war.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said two days before the NATO bombing, I wasn't able to go to work because I was in physical danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanians were doctors in Suva Reka? Apart from you, how many others were there?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact numbers, but there were 20 to 25 Albanian doctors in the clinic of Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they afraid too, or had they been appointed as members in these medical teams?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the creation of these medical teams. This is the first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the burning of Serb houses in the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned from 28th -- on the 28th of June from Albania, in 1999. That is three weeks after the end of the war, after the agreement was signed. The reason why I was late was that I had a small child --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we'll get on much better, just answer yes or no. Do you know about the burning of Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned, I saw some houses of Serbs burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a Serb house that hadn't been burnt in Suva Reka? Now.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are a lot, a lot. But there are Albanians now living in these houses. Albanians whose houses were burned are living there, and people who are unable to renovate their houses are living in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the houses that weren't forcibly taken over by the Albanians were burnt; is that right? The Serb houses, I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said some houses of Serbs in Suhareke I saw burned. Most of them, and also in most of the public housing, Albanians are living.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where are the Serbs from Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think they are in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a Serb left in Suva Reka now?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one. Not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as their houses are concerned, they were either taken over by the Albanians or burnt. Those are the two variations; right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this situation that they were taken is a sufficient one. I'm saying that Albanians are now living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't expect you to say anything like that, but I just wanted to take note of the fact that those who were forcibly taken over are inhabited now and the rest were burnt. But the fact is that there is not a single Serb in Suva Reka. Do you have any idea how many Serbs were killed and kidnapped after the 10th of June, that is to say, after your arrival there in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in Suhareke on 28th of June, three weeks after the signing of the agreement. I came very late. What happened in those three weeks, I'm not able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have no idea how many Serbs were killed and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- abducted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I raise a point? Your Honour, I reserve comments about the cross-examination by this accused generally for later, but I see the time, and it must be possible that the Chamber will be drawing matters to a conclusion. Perhaps at the break. I don't know. The accused has yet, as I understand it, to cross-examine on the central issue in this case, and I have in mind that the Court drew to his attention his ability to do so under Rule 90, and obviously it's going to help in the joining of issues if he can identify his case and cross-examine on that rather than on matters that may, many of them, be peripheral and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with the scope of cross-examination generally when we deal with administrative matters, and it would be helpful to hear from the amicus on that too, and we'll hear from the Prosecution. We note that there has been a very great deal of cross-examination about matters which are certainly not central to the witness's evidence. At this stage, we are not going to require the accused to ask any questions. It's a matter for him how he conducts his examination. But this examination should conclude in ten minutes, Mr. Milosevic. You will have had then over two hours cross-examining. In particular, you should ask in that time, if you have any questions you want to ask, with events of what this witness said he saw on the 25th and 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we differ as to what is essential and what is not. Our views differ on that point. Because that side over there with the false indictment has endeavoured to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to explain how the Albanians were subjugated, how they lived in a difficult fashion from 1989 to the NATO aggression, which saved them. And now we hear from the witness here that all that wasn't so. He did his regular university training, and all the other Albanians, who were a majority, that he got a job, that he did his specialist training, that he went to Prizren and other towns, went back to Belgrade and then continued in his job, continued working. They are all essential, vital questions. Now, this pivotal point, this pivotal question that the Prosecution wishes to impose as being pivotal, is what I said in my opening statement, that that false indictment is endeavouring to turn about notorious facts, such as the 78-day aggression and bombing and the KLA activities be denied through witnesses, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to stop you. We've heard these points. At this stage, we're dealing with cross-examination of this witness. Now, in the ten minutes remaining, is there anything more you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask questions for as long as I'm given an opportunity to ask questions, and I don't understand why you are limiting me in doing so. It is difficult to make a selection of questions now, but I see that this is a unique case in the world, where a Tribunal, even an unlawful one, openly stands on the side of terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you cautioned the policemen -- no. I have a question before that. Let me start again. You said that policemen went round in groups on that day, stormed houses, burnt down doors, and so on.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to that critical day that you have been talking about, when they stormed your house, and the day before that as well.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question was: You heard shooting in the house in which a number of people were killed, but you saw nothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that the witness [as interpreted] was not concentrating on what I was saying. He was not interested in listening to what I said I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we'll get on more quickly if you don't comment, please. Now, you've been asked a question. Could you just answer it.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events that took place, I saw these in the yard, the events in the yard, and not in the house, at a distance of ten metres. I saw the Serbian police killing civilians, innocent civilians, unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shots were in the house and that the policemen were there shooting. I listened to you very carefully. I listened to what you said very carefully, so in addition to what you were saying about the yard.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also heard shots in the house, room by room, and the house was quickly enveloped by smoke and flame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you sure that nobody shot at the policemen when they entered the house?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there no weapons in the house at all?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were no weapons, but the police who came did not come to look for weapons; they came to kill Albanian civilians, men and women, children and pregnant women. The reason, the sole reason, was because they were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're an Albanian too.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't kill you.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, how do you arrive at the conclusion that they had come to kill the Albanians, whereas you, as an Albanian, was not killed?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they went into the other people's house, not my house, and my family was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They came to your house too.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to my house on the next day. This was another group of policemen. They came with another duty: to burn my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there an Albanian family without any weapons in Kosovo today, now?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether Albanian families have weapons or not. I say that I don't have weapons in my house, and I didn't have before the war, and never have. I have always considered guns as piles of iron that cause disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to you personally. You said that they stormed houses, broke down the doors, set fire to them, and then you explained to us that you opened the doors for them. So they did not break down your door; you opened your own front door. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I opened the door myself, which wasn't broken by the first kick from the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you warned them to behave properly, and that after that warning, they did behave in a proper manner, or at least more properly.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of good behaviour is it when they ask for a thousand marks to save a house and to save the lives of the family and then to burn the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am just taking note of what you yourself said, and that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. After the start of this dialogue between me and the policemen, they seemed to calm down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they asked for all your money - I wrote that down and put it in quotation marks - all your money, and you said you wouldn't give them anything else because they would carry out what they had in mind to do, and that then they released you.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they let you go, although you didn't give them, as you yourself said, all the money, and you cautioned them to behave well, and they let you go nonetheless. And then, to focus on vital issues, you said that you made a very difficult decision, the most difficult decision you had ever had to make in your life, and that was to go to Albania. I'm jumping over the four days you spent in prison -- in Prizren, I'm sorry. Prizren. And now you have to decide between two things, because it is quite obvious that we're dealing with a key question here of showing how allegedly the Serb authorities deported the Albanians. Now, you had to decide. Did you yourself decide to go to Albania or were you deported to Albania by the Serb authorities? Because both things can't be true.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I explained well yesterday why I went to Albania, and I can say again it was the most difficult decision in my life. But to stay in Kosova was a dangerous thing for Albanians at that time. I thought to go to Albania to save my life and the lives of my family, and when all this was over, I would return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into your motives. All I'm saying is that you yourself decided to go to Albania. It wasn't that the Serb authorities deported you, because you said you made that decision, and I assume that you were telling the truth when you said that. The reason you mentioned later on was that you were going so that they should not discover that you had been an eyewitness to some of their, as you explained here, misdeeds. And the police who let you go, who let you leave Suva Reka, undoubtedly knew that you had been there the previous day. So I cannot find anything logical in your explanation, because if they knew that you were an eyewitness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You've got a question. The question, I take it, is: Why did the police let you go the day before if you fear that they might have decided to kill you if you were an eyewitness, or to harm you? Can you help or not?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police released me after taking a thousand marks from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the interpreters allow us, we will go another five minutes before the break. Mr. Milosevic, you've got another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very difficult for me to choose the questions from all the ones I've got here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you didn't give him all -- give them all the money they asked for, but they let you go nevertheless. You were an eyewitness, but they let you go nevertheless. Now, what can you deduce from this? Did they want to kill you, or did they want to let you go?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can't give an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it's not for him. It would be for them to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say that the Albanians did not flee because of the bombing, that they did not flee because of the conflicts on the terrain between the army and the KLA, but that they fled exclusively because they were being persecuted by the Serb police and the army of Yugoslavia. That is the gist of your conclusion, is it?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the residents of the town of Suhareke left because of the 50 victims who died in Suhareke that day and the victims who died in the village of Trnje where men and women, unarmed, were killed. This was a message to the population, "Go, because you are in danger."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The population got that message because of the war activities and operations. Do you consider that these activities and operations were also a message to the inhabitants and population to take shelter from the war operations?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then -- then they could have taken shelter in their own homes and not left Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And if nearby, near their homes there were conflicts and operations going on between the army and police and the KLA, do you still consider that they could have taken cover and been safe in their own homes without falling casualty in these conflicts?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't living in such places. Yes. There was never fighting near my house in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now with respect to fighting between the army and the KLA, or the police and the KLA, add to that the bombing, the NATO bombing in support of the KLA. And when you add all this together, do you consider that that was the message sent out to the population, to flee from the danger that it was exposed to?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The people were only afraid of the Serbian police and army. This was the reason why they were forced to leave Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the bombing was no factor at all. They weren't afraid of any bombing.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not afraid of the NATO bombing. I said we saw the NATO bombing, and we welcomed it with joy. We were convinced that the NATO bombs in Kosova would bring freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see how many Albanian corpses were taken out of the rubble and ruins in Pristina, Prizren, and other towns that were bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's already dealt with these matters, and that -- and that brings the conclusion -- that brings -- Mr. Milosevic, that is now quarter past eleven. That brings the cross-examination to an end, in our judgement. We will now adjourn until quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question, just one more question, Mr. May, please. Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One more. One.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When, where, and to whom did you give statements about what happened? And when I say -- I mean the authorities of this institution which is filing the indictment. Where and when and to whom did you make these statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember well. I made my first statement while I was a refugee in Albania and my second statement about a year ago, in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would need just a few minutes for my own cross-examination. Just a few minutes after the break if - with the Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can I just ask you for your indulgence for a brief explanation? You were able to see that we intervened only on a few occasions, asking questions and participating and questioning the witness, and we were guided in this - at least, I speak on my own behalf - by the fact that, as you know, Mr. Milosevic refuses to accept any documents from the Tribunal, including the witness statements, the statements of the witnesses provided previously to the OTP. So therefore, up until now, we only focused on vital questions which Mr. Milosevic was not aware of because they are contained in these previous witness statements. And now I would like to put just one question, which is a vital, pivotal one, concerning this witness's testimony, and this is what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, yesterday, during your testimony, you confirmed that, from a short distance, you saw four people being killed: Faton, Djedata [phoen], Sedata [phoen], Gjura; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that from a short distance, I saw two people being killed: Bujar and Sedat Berisha. The following minutes I saw that from the front part of my house -- that is, I saw on the back yard of the other house four dead people whom I could recognise. They were Fatime Berisha, Hava Berisha, Nexhat Berisha, and Faton Berisha. This is what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is how I understood it as well. However, did you, on the 21st of April, 1999, when interviewed by the investigators in Tirana, in Albania, say the following: that from the distance of ten metres, you watched and you saw how four men from that house were lined up, four men - Fatime, Faton, Nedat [phoen], Gjura - and then killed, in other words, that they were shot there at that spot?

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember to have said that precisely in Albania. If so, it must have been an error on the part of the interpreter. The truth is what I'm saying now, that I saw two men being killed, and then afterwards, four other dead persons of my relatives, who were pulled up to the dead bodies of the previous two persons whom I saw, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to signing this statement, this statement was read to you, and you apparently had no objections at the time.

utterances.speaker: AGRON BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm sure it must have been some errors in translation, even for the second part -- second time when I was read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions. I just wanted to emphasise that all the statements that have been taken from this witness have been served to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Berisha, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. That concludes it, and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld will be calling the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, the Prosecution calls as our next witness Ajmane Behrami. And while we're waiting for that witness to be brought into the courtroom, in response to the Court's request last date for an additional line indicating the counts and paragraphs, I have now prepared new copies with that on this trial summary, along with a couple of other typographical changes. So if I may, I would ask that these be distributed to the Court and the amici and the accused in place of the ones you now have. There are some minor things that I think it would be preferable if you would use this one. The other thing, before the witness actually comes into court, I'm going to ask that the declaration be read to her by someone and then translated as opposed to her attempting to read it herself. I understand the witness is unable to read and write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How can we get the declaration read to her?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I was wondering whether perhaps -- we don't have an Albanian-speaking person. Well, if it could be read in English, it could be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be read in English. Perhaps you would like to read it in English. It could be translated and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would be happy to do so. I'll just go get the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel will read the declaration to you. Could you repeat it when it's being translated by the interpreters? You'll hear that over your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Witness, would you repeat after me: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: "... the whole truth ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: "... and nothing but the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Witness, would you state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Ajmane Behrami.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I understand at present you are a 32-year-old Kosovo Albanian Muslim widow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not getting translation.

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that you have four surviving children?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: I used to have five. Now I have four.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We'll get back to that in a moment, yes. Thank you. Now, in March of 1999, do I understand correctly that you were a resident of a village called Izbica?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that is in the Srbica/Skenderaj municipality, is it?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, at that time in March of 1999, were you married?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was your husband living at home?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: My husband died.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, did something happen to your village in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was your husband at home when the incident involving your village occurred?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: The mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Doing what? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the mountains at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get back to that as well. Did your husband belong to any organisation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: He was a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And in addition to being a farmer, did he later join any organisation?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of an organisation called the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was your husband, to your knowledge, involved in any way with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did your husband -- you've already told us that your husband died in May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you find out how he died?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: I was not there. From the others, I heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you hear the circumstances under which he was killed?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: In the mountains. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Doing what? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: I know nothing. I was not there. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Let's move on a little bit and we'll get back to this. You've already told us that you were aware of the existence of a group called the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How were you aware of their involvement? Let me rephrase that. Where were they and what were they doing in the area of your village, if anything?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: In Izbica, we didn't have -- in the village, we didn't have anyone there. In the surrounding areas, yes, but I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Are you aware of any fighting that took place in the surrounding area, between the KLA and members of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No. I saw nothing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was fighting in the area?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that there was fighting in the surrounding area. I have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was your husband at any point a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And was he a member when he died?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: He was civilian. No. He was civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand you say he was a civilian, but you said he was a member of the KLA. He was in the mountains, and he died; is that correct? At the time he died, was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No, no. No. He just had taken to the mountains to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You've told us at some point your husband was a member of the KLA. When was that?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Before; in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was it during 1999 or 1998, or some other time? Are you able to give us perhaps a wide range, if you don't know the exact date?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: Not in 1998. In 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular incident that occurred that may have prompted him to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you very briefly to describe what life was like in your village prior to the outbreak of this difficulty in March of 1999. Can you describe for us what the village living conditions were like?

utterances.speaker: AJMANE BEHRAMI
utterances.text: We heard fire shots. Sorry. It was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
